title: The model's automated steps are unobservable in the Anthropic data by construction, so Prediction #1 measures the absence of chaining, not its presence
location: 7_empirics.tex Sec 7.1 (lines 26-28, 44); C_sample_construction.tex Sec C.1; chain cost in 3_shortrun.tex
claim: The engine of the paper is that inside a chain over steps l..r the worker "still prompts for and verifies only the same endpoint k+1" (4_implications.tex, discussion of eq. ca_test), so steps l..r-1 generate no separate human-AI interaction at all: their management cost a_i is "never paid." The Anthropic Economic Index observes conversations, i.e. exactly those human-initiated prompt-and-verify interactions, and maps each to an O*NET task. It follows mechanically that a step the model calls automated should produce no conversation of its own and should be coded manual in the constructed dataset, since "we treat tasks that do not appear in the Anthropic dataset, as well as those with 100% filtered conversations, as manual tasks" (C_sample_construction.tex). Consequently a run of consecutive is_ai=1 steps is a run of separately prompted and separately verified steps, which is precisely the arrangement chaining avoids. The paper measures "The observed mean AI chain length is 1.45" (7_empirics.tex line 44) over such runs. Under the model's own logic a genuine three-step chain appears in these data as at most one labeled task, i.e. chain length 1 flanked by two apparently manual steps. The stronger chaining is in reality, the shorter the measured chain length should be.
why_it_matters: Prediction #1, the first of three results and the one the abstract leads with ("AI-executed steps co-occur in chains"), is not a test of chaining and may carry the wrong sign relative to the mechanism. The placebo comparisons in Figure fig:aiChains_graphs_def1 would then establish only that Claude usage is content-correlated across adjacent tasks. Prediction #3 inherits the problem: it shows that separately prompted steps cluster, which is consistent with the model only if one abandons the automated/augmented distinction that is the paper's stated novelty.
already_addressed: Appendix C.1 ("Model Chains versus Anthropic Execution Labels") notices a weaker version of the problem, that the data sometimes show an automated task followed by a manual one, which the chain definition forbids. Its response is to pool the labels: "We therefore do not distinguish the two labels in what follows and treat both as indicating AI execution" (7_empirics.tex line 28). Pooling addresses the sequencing violation but cannot recover steps that generate no conversation at all. Nowhere does the paper ask what the model predicts the Anthropic labels should look like; Sections 4.2, 4.3 and Appendices D, G, H do not touch it.
fix: Derive the measurement equation: given the model, state what the Anthropic conversation-to-task mapping should produce for a workflow containing a chain over l..r, and which observable moment identifies chaining. The likely honest answer is that the right prediction is a hole, not a run: a labeled endpoint preceded by AI-exposed (E1/E2) but unlabeled steps. Test that pattern, computing for each occupation the frequency of [E1/E2-exposed and is_ai=0] immediately preceding [is_ai=1] and benchmarking against the same two reshuffle placebos. To keep the current test instead, the authors must show that Anthropic's classifier maps a single multi-step conversation onto several O*NET tasks, with evidence on multi-task mapping rates from the Anthropic release.

title: The signature theoretical result, overturning of comparative advantage, is never tested; Prediction #3 omits the neighbours' own exposure, so its estimates are fully consistent with pure comparative advantage plus spatially correlated AI-ability
location: 7_empirics.tex Sec 7.3, eq. (eq:DWA_regression_ai) and line 187; Table tab:DWA_regression_aiExecution_mainSample (tables/noTasksWithRepetitiveDWAs/allTasks_ai.tex); Prop prop:ca_local in 4_implications.tex
claim: Proposition 1 conditions on a specific event: "Let the human hold the comparative advantage on step k, so that m_k < a_k/q_k." The empirical analogue is a focal step that is NOT AI-exposed. Equation (eq:DWA_regression_ai) never conditions on it; the paper only notes "In the implementation we also control for the step t's AI exposure status" (line 187), a level shift with no interaction, no split sample, and no separate table. No specification anywhere estimates the neighbour effect on the subsample of unexposed focal steps. Worse, the neighbours' exposure is not controlled at all: grepping 7_empirics.tex, D_tables_and_robustness.tex, F, G and H returns no neighbour-exposure control. Since a neighbour's is_ai is largely determined by that neighbour's AI-ability, and AI-ability is spatially correlated along any workflow, the surviving AMEs of 0.05-0.06 in columns (2)-(4) are exactly what a textbook comparative-advantage model with correlated exposure predicts, with no chaining. One binary E1 dummy for the focal step cannot absorb this, and it says nothing about q_{k-1} and q_{k+1}.
why_it_matters: Prediction #3 is the only test capable of separating the chaining model from the standard task model, and as specified it does not. Without it the empirical section supports the proposition that AI-ability is spatially autocorrelated, which is neither news nor the paper's theory. The abstract's central claim, "a step at which humans hold an advantage in isolation may still be automated when it sits beside strong AI-performing steps," has no empirical counterpart.
already_addressed: Section 4.1 asserts the overturning result "is precisely the variation we exploit in Section 7.3," so the authors believe the test is there. Appendix D.3 adds a GPT-filtered similarity sample and an is_automated dependent variable; Appendix G re-runs the logit on frequency-pruned samples; neither conditions on focal non-exposure nor adds neighbour exposure. Appendix H states Prediction #3 cannot be run externally at all (only 9 of 137 DWAs contain both an executed and a non-executed step). The paper never reports the exposure-by-execution cross-tab (Figure fig:occupation_ai_share gives the two marginals separately), so the reader cannot see how many unexposed steps are AI-executed, the count on which the entire overturning claim rests.
fix: Three feasible additions. (1) Report the 2x2 task-level cross-tab of E1/E2 exposure against is_ai; the unexposed-and-executed cell is the overturning sample and its size determines whether a test exists. (2) Re-estimate eq. (eq:DWA_regression_ai) on the unexposed-focal subsample with DWA fixed effects and put it in the main text; this is the direct test of Proposition 1(i). (3) Add prev_is_exposed, next_is_exposed, prev2_is_exposed and next2_is_exposed to every column so the neighbour is_ai coefficient is identified from neighbours that are equally AI-able but differ in realized execution. If the effect survives (2) and (3) the paper has its headline result; if not, Prediction #3 must be reframed as evidence of spatial correlation in AI-ability.

title: Proposition 2's constant-factor bound licenses no cross-workflow comparison, and the empirical fragmentation index equals the theoretical index only at a parameter point where fragmentation cannot affect the AI-execution share
location: 4_implications.tex Sec 4.2, Prop prop:fragmentation and line 187; 7_empirics.tex Sec 7.2 lines 89-115, eq. (eq:fragmentation_index_regression); A_omitted_proofs.tex Sec A.2
claim: Two distinct gaps. (a) Proposition 2 states (1/8)OPT <= FI <= (5/4)OPT, tightened to (1/4)OPT <= FI <= (5/4)OPT when m_i >= 1. A two-sided constant-factor bound with a 5-to-10-fold spread implies nothing about the ordering of OPT across workflows: workflow A with FI=1.0 may have OPT=8 while workflow B with FI=1.2 has OPT=0.96. Yet Section 7.2 regresses across occupations and reads beta_2 < 0 as confirming that "workflows for which the fragmentation index is high will tend to yield less benefit from AI automation." That comparative static is not in the proposition. (b) EFI is not FI. Setting m_i = a_i = 1, q_i = 1 for E1/E2 steps and q_i = 0 for E0 steps in expression (eq:fragmentation) reduces realized fragmentation to (# unexposed steps) + (# maximal runs of exposed steps), which divided by m is exactly the EFI of the five-task example in Section 7.2. So EFI is FI at a degenerate deterministic calibration, which voids the mechanism twice: with q=1 on exposed steps the expectation that gives FI its content disappears, and with a_i = 1 <= m_i every exposed step is worth augmenting standalone, so the AI-execution share equals the exposure share regardless of arrangement and beta_2 = 0 is the model's own prediction there. Finally, the LHS of (eq:fragmentation_index_regression) is the AI-execution share while Proposition 2 is about cost; no result in the paper connects FI to the share of steps AI-executed.
why_it_matters: Prediction #2 is the only occupation-level test and the one that survives the external APQC validation, so it carries much of the empirical weight. As written, the theorem invoked is about a different object (cost, not execution share) and provides no cross-workflow ordering, while the measure used coincides with the theoretical index exactly where the predicted effect is zero. This reads as an empirical measure wearing the theory's name.
already_addressed: Section 7.2 concedes "we abstract from heterogeneity in tasks' underlying cost profiles, which are unobserved in our data" (line 106). Section 4.2 has one anticipatory sentence: "Where an isolated exposed step is not worth augmenting on its own, a case the model equally permits, dispersion suppresses AI execution outright rather than merely making it dearer, and it is that margin the AI-execution shares of Section 7 pick up" (line 187). That names the required knife-edge (a_i/q_i > m_i for isolated exposed steps) but proves nothing, and sits in tension with the EFI's own construction, which assumes every exposed step is chainable and executable. Appendix D.2 and Appendix G vary the EFI definition and the sample but never this mapping. The 1/8-to-5/4 ordering issue is raised nowhere.
fix: State and prove a proposition with the AI-execution share on the left: under stated conditions on (m_i, a_i, q_i), the expected number of AI-executed steps is decreasing in a dispersion measure of exposed steps, holding the number of exposed steps fixed. Second, establish co-monotonicity of FI and OPT numerically, since the constants do not deliver it: simulate workflows from a plausible (m, a, q) distribution and report the rank correlation between FI and OPT. Third, state in Section 7.2 that EFI = FI/m at q in {0,1}, m_i = a_i = 1, and report a version computed with nondegenerate q = alpha^d calibrated to the E1/E2/E0 tiers, so the empirical index carries the probabilistic content the theorem is about.

title: The one confound that would generate all three predictions at once, an LLM ordering that places semantically similar tasks adjacently, is never controlled for; the APQC validation relocates it rather than removing it
location: H_external_validation.tex lines 10-14 and Sec H.2 lines 336-380; 7_empirics.tex Sec 7.4; E_gpt_prompts.tex Prompt #1
claim: The paper itself states the alternative: "An LLM asked to arrange a list of tasks may place semantically similar items next to one another, encoding topical similarity instead of production logic. Since AI exposure and execution are themselves correlated with what a task is about, such an ordering could manufacture the contiguity we document without any underlying sequence." It then addresses it with prompt robustness, frequency pruning, APQC/4TU precedence recovery, and re-estimation of Predictions #1 and #2 on APQC's documented orderings. None of these is a control for semantic adjacency in the main sample. Every placebo in the paper (within-occupation position reshuffle; within-major-group task reassignment) destroys semantic adjacency along with sequence, so each rejects "the ordering is random" and none rejects "the ordering is topical." The APQC re-test does use an exogenous ordering, but its labels are assigned by nearest-neighbour cosine similarity in all-mpnet-base-v2 space with a 0.73 threshold: "embed each leaf element and each labeled O*NET task ... and match every step to its nearest task by cosine similarity." Adjacent steps in an APQC process group are topically closer than reshuffled ones, so they match to embedding-neighbouring O*NET tasks and inherit correlated labels; the reported z = 5.4 and z = 9.7 against reshuffle nulls are exactly what that predicts with zero chaining economics. Prediction #3, the test most vulnerable to the confound, cannot be run on APQC at all.
why_it_matters: If the ordering encodes topic, then Prediction #1 (label contiguity), Prediction #2 (fewer exposure blocks when exposed tasks are topically tight) and Prediction #3 (neighbour correlation) all follow from one non-economic fact about how GPT-5-mini sorts a list, and the paper has no empirical content. The paper's own diagnostic leaves ample room for this: "the model's orderings agree with each other at an average pairwise tau of 0.79, well above the 0.53 they achieve against APQC," i.e. the instrument is markedly more self-consistent than accurate.
already_addressed: Appendix H is explicitly built around this concern and does substantial work: it names the mechanism verbatim, benchmarks the ordering procedure against 345 documented PCF branches and five event logs, and re-runs Predictions #1 and #2 on documented sequences. What remains missing is any control for, or placebo preserving, semantic adjacency in the main O*NET sample, and any way to keep the label transfer in the APQC exercise from reintroducing the same correlation. Appendix F (prompt robustness) and Appendix G (frequency pruning) do not speak to it, and Section 7.1 explicitly concedes the placebos "do not establish that the GPT task orderings we use are the 'right' ones."
fix: Two cheap exercises. (1) A semantic-adjacency placebo: for each occupation construct an ordering that maximizes embedding similarity between consecutive tasks (greedy nearest-neighbour or a TSP path over task embeddings, with no workflow reasoning) and re-run all three tests on it. If mean chain length, the EFI coefficient and the neighbour AME are as large under this purely topical ordering as under the GPT ordering, the results are not about sequence. (2) Add the focal-neighbour embedding cosine similarity as a control in eq. (eq:DWA_regression_ai) and as a covariate in the fragmentation regression, and report how much of the effect survives. For APQC, additionally report results restricted to step pairs whose matched O*NET tasks are not embedding-neighbours, to break the label-transfer channel.

title: Two headline theoretical claims, monotonicity in AI quality (Prop 1(ii)) and non-monotone returns to AI quality (Sec 4.3), are promised in the abstract and never confronted with data, and the stated excuse does not cover them
location: 0_main.tex abstract line 70; 4_implications.tex Sec 4.3 and Prop prop:ca_local(ii); 7_empirics.tex lines 2-6; C_sample_construction.tex line 13
claim: The abstract advertises "that marginal improvements in AI quality can generate non-monotone productivity gains as longer chains become viable," and Section 6 elevates it to "a microfoundation for the productivity J-curve phenomenon" yielding "testable predictions on when and how AI-driven productivity gains trigger structural reorganization in labor markets." Neither this nor Proposition 1(ii)'s monotone comparative static in (q_{k-1}, q_k, q_{k+1}) appears among the three predictions taken to data. Section 7 lists exactly three and defends the omission of everything else on long-run grounds: "not enough time has passed since the AI tools became widely available for such reorganization to have worked its way into the data we observe" (line 4). That defence covers Section 5's job redesign but not Section 4.3, which is derived inside the same fixed-job short-run cost minimization as Predictions #1-#3 and whose comparative static is in alpha, not in the horizon. The empirics are cross-sectional by choice: "We use the May 2023 release of O*NET" plus a single vintage of the Anthropic index, with no time index anywhere in Section 7.
why_it_matters: An abstract claim with no empirical counterpart and no stated reason for its absence is a standard reason a general-interest referee concludes the theory and the empirics are two papers stapled together. It also forgoes the only prediction that discriminates the chaining model on a dimension other than adjacency: alpha-driven regime switching is a signature no correlated-exposure story reproduces, so testing it would answer several of the objections above at once.
already_addressed: Appendix A.3 proves the general non-monotonicity result (Lemma lem:reorg_threshold) and Appendix D.1 tabulates the two-step example, so the theory side is complete. Section 7.3 contains one forward-looking sentence, "It is possible that with improvements in AI quality, chains become longer and execution status of more distant neighbors becomes more relevant for the execution mode of the focal task," which names the right test and declines to run it. The paper nowhere states that the prediction is untestable or explains why the successive Anthropic Economic Index releases are not used.
fix: Use the successive Anthropic Economic Index vintages as variation in alpha with the task ordering held fixed. (1) Proposition 1(ii): a task coded is_ai=1 in an early vintage should not revert to is_ai=0 in a later one above a classification-noise benchmark, and the reversion rate should be lower for tasks with AI-executed neighbours. (2) Section 4.3: the between-vintage change in an occupation's AI-execution share should concentrate in low-EFI occupations and should arrive as extensions of existing runs rather than as isolated additions, i.e. mean run length should rise faster than the number of maximal runs. If the vintages are too close together to identify this, say so explicitly in Section 7 rather than leaving an abstract claim untested and unmentioned.

title: The Prediction #3 logit contains no occupation fixed effect, so occupation-level AI adoption is ruled out only graphically by the reshuffle, never in the reported table
claim: The reported columns include SOC major-group FE (2), SOC minor-group FE (3), DWA FE (4), the number of same-DWA tasks in the focal occupation (5-6), the focal task's exposure status and the occupation's task count. There is no occupation (O*NET-SOC code) fixed effect in any column. SOC minor groups pool many occupations, so a common occupation-level Claude adoption shock, in which some occupations' workers use Claude for everything and others for nothing, mechanically correlates neighbour is_ai with focal is_ai within occupation and is not absorbed. That is a fully specified alternative model containing no chaining. Column (4)'s DWA FE addresses task-type heterogeneity, the orthogonal dimension.
why_it_matters: Without an occupation FE the reader cannot tell whether the surviving 0.05 AME is a within-workflow adjacency effect or a between-occupation adoption effect. Since occupation-level adoption is also the leading non-chaining explanation for Prediction #2, the objection propagates across both tests.
already_addressed: The within-occupation position reshuffle placebo in Figure fig:DWA_regression_aiExecution_mainSample does hold each occupation's set of execution labels fixed and is therefore informative against this alternative, and the observed AME lies to the right of the null. But it appears only as four histograms, never as a coefficient with a standard error, and it is not equivalent to an occupation FE, since the null is centred on the reshuffled coefficient rather than on zero. Appendix D.3 and Appendix G add samples and dependent variables but no occupation FE, and the omission is not discussed.
fix: Add a column with occupation fixed effects to Table tab:DWA_regression_aiExecution_mainSample, and occupation-plus-DWA fixed effects if the 4,096-observation sample supports it. Because a logit with occupation FE on that sample hits an incidental-parameters problem, report a linear probability model with occupation FE alongside, or a conditional logit. State the identifying variation explicitly: within an occupation, across positions, comparing tasks in the same DWA.

title: The exposure variable is E1 in the regression but E1-or-E2 in the fragmentation index it is meant to condition on, and the joint distribution of exposure and execution is never reported
location: C_sample_construction.tex line 16; 7_empirics.tex lines 110-113 and the note to Table tab:fragmentation_index_regression_exposure; H_external_validation.tex line 353
claim: Appendix C states the paper's convention: "we treat tasks with a human-assigned E1 label as exposed to AI and those with E0 or E2 labels as unexposed to AI," calling it "a conservative measure." Section 7.2 builds the EFI on a different set: "We count as AI-exposed both E1- and E2-exposed tasks, which together account for 44% of the tasks in the dataset." The table note then says "'AI Exposure' denotes the share of AI-exposed (E1) steps" while the control is "the number of AI-exposed (E1 or E2) steps." A single regression thus uses one definition for the exposure regressor and a wider one for both the index and the count control, so steps the exposure variable calls unexposed are treated as chainable by the index. Section 7.3 says only "we also control for the step t's AI exposure status" without saying which definition. Appendix H reports "46%" AI-exposed in the O*NET universe against the 44% of Section 7.2. Separately, Figure fig:occupation_ai_share reports the marginal distributions of exposure share and execution share; the 2x2 joint distribution appears nowhere.
why_it_matters: The reader cannot reconstruct what beta_1 and beta_2 in Table tab:fragmentation_index_regression_exposure are conditional on, nor check the internal consistency of the EFI. The missing joint distribution is more consequential: it is the one table that shows how much of the paper's phenomenon exists, namely how many unexposed steps are AI-executed and how many exposed steps are not.
already_addressed: A footnote in Section 7.2 explains why E2 is included in the EFI ("restricting attention to E1-exposed tasks alone (14% of tasks) would leave potential AI chains too sparse for fragmentation to be meaningfully measured"), which justifies the wider definition in the index but does not reconcile it with the narrower one used for the regressor. Nothing in the paper addresses the missing cross-tab or the 44%/46% discrepancy.
fix: Report both EFI Definition 1 and the exposure regressor under a single stated exposure convention, with the alternative convention in an appendix table, and state in Section 7.3 which convention the focal-task exposure control uses. Add a 2x2 table of E1/E2 exposure by is_ai at the task level, and the same cross-tab by SOC major group, early in Section 7.
